new_platform_errors: States PBKDF2 in Workers' SubtleCrypto is 'capped at 100,000 iterations' — this is not a spec/runtime-enforced limit; OWASP recommends a 600,000+ minimum and Workers does not impose a hard 100,000 ceiling on PBKDF2 iteration count

Review states CacheService 'is capped at 1,000 items with early eviction of whichever entries have the soonest remaining TTL' — Google's Apps Script CacheService reference does not document any such fixed 1,000-item cap or a soonest-TTL eviction policy; this is a fabricated quota/mechanism, not a real platform constraint.

Review's Finding #2 claims `clasp open --webapp` is invalid in both clasp major versions (asserting 2.x used `--web` and 3.x renamed it to `open-web-app`), but `--webapp` is actually a documented valid flag on clasp's `open` command (used to open the deployed web app URL), so this 'correction' is itself a fabricated platform claim.

Review states LockService.getDocumentLock() 'returns null outside a document context.' In Apps Script, getDocumentLock() does not return null when called outside a bound document; it returns a Lock object, and the failure instead surfaces as a thrown exception when the lock is actually used/waited on outside a document-bound script context.

Finding #3's correction proposes a 'text/formula field marked Unique/External ID' for Shot_Key__c — Salesforce does not allow the Unique or External ID attributes on formula fields; those attributes are only available on non-formula Text/Number/Email custom fields, so a formula-field version of this fix would not be implementable as described.

Finding 2 claims 'a plain Apex DML statement only locks a row during that statement's own execution' — this is wrong. In Salesforce, a lock acquired by a DML operation is held for the remainder of the enclosing transaction (until commit or rollback), not just for the duration of that single statement. The recommended fix (adding `FOR UPDATE` to the initial SELECT) is correct, but the stated reason misdescribes how long DML-acquired locks actually last.

R7_gas_1.how: Plan keeps board/mark server-side keyed to Session.getActiveUser() identity (never client-supplied), so even arbitrary apiExec calls can't spoof seat/turn; verification step explicitly requires testing a raw apiExec probe fails out-of-turn/wrong-mark plays.

R7_gas_2.how: Plan explicitly names apiExec/srv as not a trust boundary but only closes it by arguing tic-tac-toe has no hidden state; it never adds server-side redaction of opponent fleet data before sending records to clients, so for a hidden-fleet game the same arbitrary-code-exec path still exposes hidden state.

R7_gas_3.how: Plan explicitly says the game (TTT) has no hidden info, so it only addresses turn-authority via Session email; it never considers that apiExec/new Function lets any authenticated player call arbitrary server code to read hidden state (e.g. opponent's ship positions) directly from PropertiesService, so the read/confidentiality risk for hidden fleets is neither identified nor mitigated.
